transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: FinchBank x Redwood Inference — Security/Compliance Review (Model Change Logs + Auditability)
Date: 2026-02-11
Start time: 18:00 UTC
Duration: 54 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Ava Chen, Marcus Lin, Kevin Osei, Jordan Lee, Connor O'Brien
FinchBank: Rita Shah (GRC / Vendor Risk), Tom Alvarez (Security Architect), Evan Cho (Platform Eng), Nina Patel (Compliance), Speaker 6 (Procurement)

---
Summary (auto-generated)
FinchBank reviewed Redwood’s approach to auditable model metadata changes and customer-visible model release notes (“model changelog”). Discussion focused on who can edit vs approve vs publish notes, evidence of immutability/tamper resistance, retention periods, and how Redwood handles corrections. Redwood outlined an event-based audit trail for model metadata create/update/deprecate and changelog publish actions, with SIEM-friendly exports and role-based access controls. FinchBank requested sample event payloads and formal retention language.

Topics (auto-generated)
- Model metadata change audit events (who/what/when)
- Changelog publication workflow (draft → in_review → published)
- Correction/rollback (supersede entries, preserve history)
- Retention & immutability (WORM/tamper-evident, export)
- RBAC, SSO/SAML, approval separation of duties
- Customer access: console, API fields, feeds (RSS/JSON)

Questions (auto-generated)
- Can Redwood prove that published release notes cannot be edited without leaving evidence?
- What is the retention period for model change audit events and customer-visible notes?
- Who at Redwood can approve/publish customer-visible notes, and is there a two-person rule?
- Can FinchBank export change events to Splunk/Chronicle and correlate with tickets?

---
Transcript

[00:00] Ava Chen: Cool. Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Ava from Redwood. We’ve got Marcus from security engineering, Kevin who owns audit and retention stuff, Jordan who’s been working on the RBAC side, and Connor from release engineering.

[00:12] Rita Shah: Great, thanks Ava. I’m Rita in vendor risk. I have Tom, Nina, and Evan on as well.

[00:20] Tom Alvarez: Hey.

[00:22] Evan Cho: Hi.

[00:24] Nina Patel: Hello.

[00:26] Ava Chen: The agenda we got from your questionnaire is basically: (1) auditability of model changes, (2) retention and immutability, and (3) who can approve customer-visible release notes. We can also cover how you’d consume this—console versus API—if that helps.

[00:43] Rita Shah: Yes. And just to be explicit, we’ve had issues with vendors where the “model” changed but we couldn’t get evidence of when, who approved it, and what the impact was. So we’re looking for strong change-management controls.

[01:01] Ava Chen: Yep, understood.

[01:04] Marcus Lin: Maybe I’ll start with the high-level. Redwood is putting model/version metadata into a canonical registry and emitting signed change events when metadata changes—create, update, deprecate—and also when customer-facing release notes are published. Those events are what we use both for internal audit and to generate the customer-visible changelog.

[01:28] Tom Alvarez: When you say “signed,” like cryptographic signed?

[01:31] Marcus Lin: The intent is tamper-evident. The event stream is append-only on our side. Kevin can speak to the mechanics, but from a customer perspective: every published entry references immutable event IDs and timestamps, and corrections don’t overwrite—they supersede.

[01:48] Kevin Osei: Yeah. The simplest way to explain it: the record of “what happened” is an append-only audit log with unique event IDs. If we need to fix wording in a release note, we publish a new entry that supersedes the old one, and the old one remains accessible for audit with a “superseded_by” pointer.

[02:09] Rita Shah: Okay. We will need that spelled out. Our auditors ask “show that history is preserved.”

[02:16] Kevin Osei: Yep.

[02:18] Evan Cho: Can you define “model change” here? Is it weights change? Is it quantization? Is it routing?

[02:26] Jordan Lee: Good question. In our metadata we track version identity and provenance—like model artifact hash, upstream base model version, quantization profile, context window, compatibility flags (tool calling etc). The changelog entries are generated from changes to that metadata. So: if we swap a quant profile or update the served artifact, it’s a new version or at minimum a metadata update with an event.

[02:49] Evan Cho: So it’s not like the same version ID could suddenly point to different weights.

[02:54] Jordan Lee: Correct. Version IDs are immutable pointers. The policy is: if artifact changes, version changes. If it’s purely descriptive metadata, there’s still an update event, but we don’t change the underlying artifact.

[03:09] Tom Alvarez: How do you enforce that? Like technically.

[03:12] Jordan Lee: The registry validation enforces constraints. Certain fields—like artifact digest and version identity—are immutable after publish. Attempts to update those are rejected, and an audit event is logged for the attempt. (Transcription note: I said “rejected,” it might sound like “redirected.”)

[03:32] Connor O'Brien: And release engineering aligns this with release trains. We don’t allow “silent changes” during freeze windows. If something urgent happens, we use an emergency publish path that still generates the event trail.

[03:46] Rita Shah: I’m going to pause on the emergency path. We’ll come back. First: who can create and who can approve.

[03:55] Ava Chen: Yeah, let’s do RBAC.

[03:57] Rita Shah: We need segregation of duties. Ideally: engineer can draft, but another function approves. Also we need to know if support can publish.

[04:07] Jordan Lee: The workflow we’re implementing for customer-visible notes is state-based: draft → in_review → published. Roles are separate. “Metadata Editor” can draft metadata changes and draft a customer-safe summary. “Release Note Approver” can move to in_review/published. And a smaller group has “Publisher” permissions.

[04:30] Tom Alvarez: Is approver == publisher or different?

[04:33] Jordan Lee: They can be distinct. For enterprise customers we recommend two-person approval—one from product/release and one from security/compliance for sensitive categories. Internally we enforce that the actor who drafts cannot be the sole publisher for certain change types—like deprecations or policy/safety notes.

[04:53] Nina Patel: What do you mean by “sensitive categories.”

[04:56] Marcus Lin: Anything that could be interpreted as a security or policy statement, or anything that affects availability in a regulated environment—deprecations, replacements, model behavior constraints, or compatibility breaking changes.

[05:12] Rita Shah: Okay. We will likely require that for us.

[05:16] Ava Chen: And from a customer POV, you’ll see the published notes in Console and via API/feed, but not the internal-only fields.

[05:24] Tom Alvarez: That’s another concern. We need to ensure you’re not leaking internal details but also giving us enough for change approvals.

[05:31] Ava Chen: Right. The public fields are allow-listed. There’s redaction logic so internal notes never make it to the customer-facing template.

[05:40] Evan Cho: Are those templates human-written or AI-generated?

[05:43] Connor O'Brien: They’re templated. The generator is deterministic based on a diff of allowed fields. Humans can edit the summary text, but edits are tracked and require approval before publish.

[05:59] Rita Shah: So if someone edits the text, we want to know who did it.

[06:03] Kevin Osei: Every step is an event: “draft created,” “text edited,” “moved to in_review,” “published,” and if corrected, “superseded.” Each event includes actor identity, timestamp, and the object IDs (model_id, version_id, changelog_entry_id).

[06:23] Tom Alvarez: Actor identity meaning a human user? Or could be a service account.

[06:27] Kevin Osei: Both. For automation it’s a service principal, but it’s still an authenticated identity with scoped permissions. Human approvals are human identities. We support SSO on our side so those map back to our IdP.

[06:42] Nina Patel: Do you do SAML?

[06:44] Jordan Lee: Yes, SAML SSO for console and admin tools. And we can enforce MFA requirements via the IdP.

[06:52] Speaker 6: Sorry, procurement here—do you have SOC 2?

[06:56] Marcus Lin: We’re SOC 2 Type II. We can share the report under NDA. Also ISO 27001 is in progress, but SOC 2 is current.

[07:06] Rita Shah: Okay, thanks. Back to retention and immutability. Our baseline is 7 years retention for change records. Can you do that?

[07:17] Kevin Osei: For audit events, yes we can retain for 7 years in our audit log storage tier. For customer-visible notes, those are published artifacts—effectively indefinitely, but we can commit to a minimum retention period contractually.

[07:33] Tom Alvarez: Indefinitely is fine but we need “cannot delete” language.

[07:37] Kevin Osei: We have to be careful with “cannot delete” legally, but we can do “immutable retention” / “append-only” / “tamper-evident” language. Deletion would require a break-glass process with audit trail.

[07:55] Rita Shah: Do you have WORM storage?

[07:58] Kevin Osei: We use append-only storage semantics and object lock equivalents in our archive tier. I’ll send the exact wording. The key is: you can’t modify an existing event; you can only add a new event.

[08:14] Evan Cho: If we ask “show me all model changes that impacted FinchBank,” can you filter by tenant?

[08:21] Jordan Lee: Two flavors. The model catalog changes are global events (model versions available). Tenant-specific rollouts—like if you were on Dedicated with pinned versions—are separate operational events in the rollout system. But the published note references the version, and in console you’d see what version you had at what time.

[08:43] Evan Cho: Right now we’re evaluating private VPC deployment.

[08:46] Ava Chen: Yep.

[08:48] Evan Cho: So would we have access to the audit log in our environment?

[08:52] Marcus Lin: For Private deployments, we support exporting audit events to your SIEM, and in some setups you can host the audit store in your environment. For Hosted/Dedicated, we provide export and API access.

[09:07] Tom Alvarez: Can you integrate to Splunk?

[09:09] Kevin Osei: We can export in JSON with stable field names, and deliver via webhook/S3-style drop, depending. Most customers send that to Splunk/Chronicle/Elastic. We’ll share the field mapping.

[09:25] Rita Shah: We’ll need example payloads. Including the changelog publish event.

[09:30] Kevin Osei: Yep.

[09:31] Ava Chen: And to make it concrete, when a model version is updated, the API responses will include the resolved model_version and a changelog URL so your app teams can correlate.

[09:44] Evan Cho: That’s the header you mentioned?

[09:46] Ava Chen: Exactly. It shows what version served the request.

[09:50] Tom Alvarez: Going back, you mentioned competitors—AWS and Azure. We’ve seen their model endpoints change silently sometimes. We want to avoid that.

[09:58] Ava Chen: That’s the point of this effort.

[10:01] Rita Shah: Okay. Let’s drill into “who can approve.” You said security/compliance can be required for sensitive categories. Is that a configurable policy?

[10:12] Jordan Lee: Internally it’s policy-driven. For customer-facing notes we have gating rules: e.g., deprecation requires Product + Release Eng approval. For certain categories we require Security reviewer. We can map that to your expectation. In the future, we can also do per-customer gating for private deployments, but that’s not in the first release.

[10:33] Nina Patel: We’d like to have at least an SLA: like 30 days notice for deprecation.

[10:38] Connor O'Brien: Yep, our default deprecation policy is 90 days for general availability models, unless it’s a security or critical reliability issue. In those cases, we’ll publish an urgent note with shorter timelines and a replacement.

[10:56] Rita Shah: And that urgent path, can you explain with evidence? Like it still goes through approval?

[11:03] Connor O'Brien: It’s a “hotfix publish” process. There’s still an approver, but the review SLA is minutes/hours not days. The system records who invoked it, why, and links to an incident ID.

[11:18] Tom Alvarez: Can the same person both invoke and approve?

[11:21] Jordan Lee: For hotfix we still require two distinct identities for publish when the category is “breaking” or “security.” For minor wording corrections, it can be one approver but it’s still logged.

[11:36] Kevin Osei: And again, corrections don’t overwrite. They supersede. So even if someone made a mistake, you can see the original plus the correction, with timestamps.

[11:47] Rita Shah: That’s good. But we need to ensure that the original isn’t visible to customers if it’s wrong.

[11:54] Ava Chen: Practically, the UI will show the latest entry with a banner like “This entry was corrected on X date,” and optionally a link to view the prior entry for audit. We can make that prior view restricted or not shown to end users depending on your needs.

[12:12] Evan Cho: For our internal auditors, we’d want access. For developers, maybe not.

[12:16] Ava Chen: Makes sense.

[12:18] Tom Alvarez: What about retention of the notes themselves. If we subscribe to RSS or JSON feed, and later a note is corrected, do we get both?

[12:27] Kevin Osei: The feed includes entries plus status. When superseded, we emit a new event/entry that references the prior. So your system can ingest both and mark one as superseded.

[12:41] Evan Cho: Cool.

[12:43] Rita Shah: Another item: do you track “who changed what fields” or just that “metadata updated.”

[12:50] Jordan Lee: We track the diff at the field level for the metadata object. For customer-safe changes, we include only public fields in the customer note, but internally the audit event includes which fields changed and the before/after (with redactions where needed).

[13:08] Tom Alvarez: Before/after values too? That’s helpful.

[13:11] Jordan Lee: For most fields, yes. For sensitive internal notes, we may store a hash or redact the full content, but still record that it changed.

[13:20] Nina Patel: What about the actual model weights? Are those in scope of the audit.

[13:25] Marcus Lin: We don’t store weights in audit logs, but we store artifact identifiers—hash/digest—so you can prove which artifact was served.

[13:34] Evan Cho: That’s what we want.

[13:37] Rita Shah: I want to make sure we can answer: “If Redwood says we pinned model X version Y, can we prove it didn’t change?”

[13:45] Ava Chen: Yes—version immutability plus the response header/field that returns the served version. And the audit trail of any changes.

[13:55] Tom Alvarez: Is the version always returned? Even streaming.

[13:59] Ava Chen: Yes, included in headers and in the response object in the SDKs.

[14:04] Evan Cho: Okay.

[14:06] Rita Shah: Next: access controls. Can any Redwood employee see our usage and correlate with model changes.

[14:15] Marcus Lin: Access is least privilege. Support access is time-bound and logged. For Dedicated/Private, data isolation is stronger. For audit events related to your account, access is restricted to specific roles.

[14:30] Tom Alvarez: Do you have an “audit of audit access.” Like who viewed logs.

[14:34] Kevin Osei: Yes, administrative access is itself audited—view/export actions generate audit events. We can include that in export too.

[14:44] Rita Shah: Great.

[14:46] (crosstalk)

[14:47] Ava Chen: Sorry, go ahead Tom.

[14:49] Tom Alvarez: I was just going to ask about data residency. We’re US-only.

[14:54] Ava Chen: Hosted can be region-pinned. Dedicated and Private can be constrained to specific regions/VPC. Audit logs follow that deployment region; for Private you can keep everything in your environment.

[15:07] Nina Patel: Okay.

[15:09] Rita Shah: Let’s talk about the changelog content. Our preference is: impact statement, compatibility, and timeline for deprecation.

[15:18] Connor O'Brien: That matches our template. We require sections like “What changed,” “Customer impact,” “Compatibility,” and “Deprecation” if applicable. We also link to dashboards/evals where appropriate.

[15:33] Evan Cho: Are eval links public? We might not want our prompts in there.

[15:37] Ava Chen: Those are Redwood’s evals, not customer prompts. But we can keep them high-level metrics.

[15:44] Rita Shah: Another thing: we don’t want internal codenames.

[15:48] Connor O'Brien: Yeah, templates forbid internal nicknames. There’s linting in docs build too.

[15:56] Tom Alvarez: Who can edit the template.

[15:58] Connor O'Brien: Engineering can propose, docs approves. It’s version-controlled. But the actual published note is generated per event.

[16:07] Rita Shah: For our audit, we need “approval happened” evidence. Is there a report.

[16:13] Kevin Osei: You can query by time range, model_id, version_id, and event type: published, superseded, deprecated. We can also provide periodic exports.

[16:25] Evan Cho: Does the API have pagination and filtering.

[16:28] Jordan Lee: Yes—cursor-based pagination, filter by model, date range, and status.

[16:34] Tom Alvarez: Any rate limiting.

[16:36] Jordan Lee: Yes, but reasonable for polling. There’s caching with ETags.

[16:44] Rita Shah: Okay. I want to make sure the approval workflow includes compliance. Nina, do you have requirements.

[16:52] Nina Patel: Mostly that policy changes are reviewed by compliance, and that retention is 7 years. Also we need to store evidence in our system.

[17:01] Rita Shah: So export is key.

[17:04] Ava Chen: Understood.

[17:06] Tom Alvarez: One more scenario: what if Redwood learns a model update had a subtle behavior change. Do you publish a note.

[17:13] Connor O'Brien: If it’s a behavior-impacting change, yes. In v1 we’re not auto-writing “quality diff narratives” but we can link to metrics. If it’s discovered later, we publish a retroactive note with the correct effective date and an explanation that it was identified after the fact.

[17:32] Rita Shah: Retroactive is okay as long as it’s logged and transparent.

[17:37] Kevin Osei: It would show “published_at” and “effective_at” separately.

[17:41] Tom Alvarez: That’s important.

[17:44] Ava Chen: Yep.

[17:46] (minor audio drop)

[17:49] Evan Cho: Sorry, I missed—did you say “effective at” is a field.

[17:53] Kevin Osei: Yes, for certain entries. So you can tell when the change took effect, versus when the note was published.

[18:02] Evan Cho: Great.

[18:05] Rita Shah: Okay. We have about ten minutes left. Let’s go to concrete deliverables: sample payload, retention language, RBAC chart.

[18:14] Ava Chen: Kevin can send retention + immutability language. Marcus can send sample audit payload. Jordan can send the role matrix.

[18:23] Tom Alvarez: Also include whether support can publish.

[18:26] Jordan Lee: Support can draft “support notes” internally, but customer-visible publish is restricted to release-note approvers/publishers. Support cannot directly publish to customer feed without approval.

[18:39] Rita Shah: Good.

[18:41] Speaker 6: Can you also send your standard DPA language for retention.

[18:45] Ava Chen: Yes, I’ll coordinate with legal.

[18:48] Tom Alvarez: And if we go Private, can we integrate the approval workflow with our own change ticketing.

[18:54] Connor O'Brien: Not automatically in v1, but we can include a “customer_ticket_id” field in the release note metadata and require it during review for Private deployments.

[19:07] Evan Cho: That’s actually huge.

[19:09] Rita Shah: Yeah, because we need to tie it to our CAB.

[19:12] Jordan Lee: We can support that as a required field in your deployment policy.

[19:18] Ava Chen: We’ll note that as a requirement.

[19:21] Tom Alvarez: One last question: do you do encryption at rest and KMS.

[19:25] Marcus Lin: Yes. For Hosted/Dedicated, encryption at rest with cloud KMS. For Private, you can use your KMS/HSM integrations.

[19:34] Nina Patel: Okay.

[19:36] Rita Shah: Great. Ava, can you summarize next steps.

[19:40] Ava Chen: Yep. We’ll send: (1) retention/tamper-evidence writeup, (2) sample audit event payloads including publish and supersede, (3) RBAC role matrix + who can approve/publish, (4) notes on hotfix publish path and how it’s audited. And Rita, you’ll confirm retention and whether you require WORM wording.

[20:00] Rita Shah: Correct.

[20:02] Ava Chen: And we’ll schedule a follow-up next week focused on mapping this to your internal change-management process, including that ticket ID field.

[20:10] Evan Cho: Works for me.

[20:12] Tom Alvarez: Thanks.

[20:13] Nina Patel: Thanks.

[20:15] Ava Chen: Thanks everyone.

(Transcript continues with light scheduling chatter; end of recording.)

---
Auto-generated Action Items
- Redwood to send sample audit event payloads (metadata update, publish, supersede)
- Redwood to send retention/immutability language (7-year option)
- FinchBank to confirm required retention and WORM requirements
- Schedule RBAC/approval follow-up
